Question title; answered by [Wikipedia: Survival of the fittest] 'Herbert Spencer first used the phrase'.
'Herbert Spencer first used the phrase, after reading Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, in his Principles of Biology (1864)'
Spencer: 'This survival of the fittest ... is that which Mr. Darwin has called "natural selection"'
'In July 1866, Alfred Russel Wallace wrote to Darwin about readers thinking that the phrase "natural selection" personified nature...'
units.note: Letters are one line of evidence. Darwin also credited Spencer in print (Variation, 1868: 'Mr. Herbert Spencer has well expressed the same idea by the Survival of the Fittest').

units.evidence: 'readers thinking that the phrase "natural selection" personified nature as "selecting" and said this misconception could be avoided "by adopting Spencer's term"'

Darwin: 'I fully agree with all that you say on the advantages of H. Spencer's excellent expression of "the survival of the fittest". This however had not occurred to me till reading your letter.'; 'In On the Origin of Species, he introduced the phrase in the fifth edition published in 1869'
units.note: 'The idea had not occurred to him' is ambiguous and can be heard as Darwin never having thought of the concept. What had not occurred to him was the advantage of Spencer's phrase. The fifth-edition date is right (he first used the phrase in Variation, 1868).
units.fix: Darwin wrote back that the advantages of Spencer's phrase had not occurred to him until he read the letter. He put the phrase in the fifth edition of the Origin, in 1869.
units.resolved: Now "the advantages of Spencer's phrase had not occurred to him"; quote extended to include Darwin's sentence about the advantages.

units.evidence: 'The biological concept of fitness is defined as reproductive success. In Darwinian terms, the phrase is best understood as "survival of the form that in successive generations will leave most copies of itself."'
units.note: The source never mentions 'strongest'. 'Never meant' is absolute (popular and Social Darwinist uses did read it as strength), and 'it means' drops 'in Darwinian terms ... best understood as'. Darwin himself glossed it as 'better designed for an immediate, local environment'.
units.fix: And in biology, "fittest" doesn't mean strongest. It is best understood as the form that leaves the most copies of itself.
units.resolved: Now "In biology, fittest does not mean strongest. It is best understood as the form that leaves the most copies of itself."
